Password-Typing Verification Across Sessions:
Distance Detectors, a One-Class SVM and a Siamese Embedding on the CMU Keystroke Benchmark

BİL462 Biometric Recognition · Final Report · Topic A5 · Bahadır İhsan Herdem (221101034), Ömer Efe Öztürk (221101059) · December 2026
Abstract. We verify users from the rhythm with which they type a fixed password, on the public CMU benchmark (51 subjects × 8 sessions × 50 entries). Three distance detectors, a one-class SVM and a shared Siamese embedding network are evaluated within a session (C1) and across sessions (C2) on 41 subjects that were never used for tuning or for training a shared model. Our replication of the original protocol reproduces the published reference results (scaled Manhattan 9.6% vs. 9.6%). Across sessions the mean EER of the best single detector is 14.3% (One-class SVM); the Siamese embedding is the best detector within a session (10.6%) but loses the most across sessions (+5.1 percentage points), so within-session results are optimistic for learned models in particular. Fusing three detectors gives 12.7% and averaging five consecutive entries 7.1%. Error rates of this size mean that keystroke rhythm is a useful second factor, not a stand-alone authenticator. A localhost demo implements the same pipeline as a password-plus-rhythm login.

1. Introduction

Problem. A password can be stolen, guessed or shoulder-surfed, but the way it is typed (how long each key is held and how quickly the next one follows) is harder to copy. Keystroke dynamics adds this behavioural check to an existing password without extra hardware. We study static, password-based verification: every subject types the same fixed password, and a per-user detector decides whether a new entry was typed by the claimed user. Typing rhythm, however, changes from day to day: people get faster, pause differently, or are tired. Results measured inside one sitting may therefore be optimistic.

Question (topic A5). How well do simple and learned detectors separate users who type the same password, and how much does performance drop across sessions? Trait: keystroke dynamics (behavioural). Data: the CMU Keystroke Dynamics Benchmark [1] only.

Contributions. (i) A from-scratch implementation of the Manhattan, scaled Manhattan and Mahalanobis detectors that reproduces the reference results of [1]; (ii) a separate within-session (C1) and cross-session (C2) evaluation with DET curves, per-user EER and subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals, plus a template-ageing curve with a fixed enrolment size; (iii) two learned models, a per-user one-class SVM and a Siamese embedding shared across users, trained on subjects disjoint from those evaluated; (iv) score fusion across detectors and across consecutive entries; (v) an error analysis; (vi) a working password-plus-rhythm login demo.

2. Literature Review

Origins. Joyce and Gupta [2] built identity signatures from inter-key latencies and compared new attempts with a mean reference (a Manhattan-type rule); Monrose and Rubin [3] studied keystroke dynamics for authentication and showed large differences between users. Benchmarking. Published results were hard to compare because studies differed in password, amount of training data, impostor data and threshold rule. Killourhy and Maxion [1] therefore collected the benchmark we use and evaluated 14 anomaly detectors under a single protocol. The best ones (scaled Manhattan, nearest-neighbour Mahalanobis, outlier count, one-class SVM) reached 9.6–10.2% mean EER; detectors that scale each feature by its variability did best, and no detector came close to the error rates required for access control. Their follow-up [6] modelled which factors drive error rates (algorithm, training amount, feature set, template updating, impostor familiarity, and the typist themself), showing that per-user variation is at least as important as the choice of detector. Learned models. One-class SVMs [5] learn a boundary around the genuine data only and were applied to keystroke novelty detection by Yu and Cho [4]. Later work moved to deep models: TypeNet [8] trains an LSTM embedding with Siamese and triplet losses on free text from large populations, and TypeFormer [9] uses Transformers for mobile typing; both learn a metric space shared by all users so that new users need only a few enrolment samples. For fixed text, Chang et al. [10] compare classical and deep classifiers, and Sasikumar and Nagarajan [11] report 94.75% accuracy and 1.0% EER on the CMU data with an LSTM ensemble. Those numbers come from 5- and 10-fold cross-validation that mixes sessions and uses impostor samples in training, i.e. a closed-set classification setting rather than the session-ordered verification protocol required here, so they are not comparable with ours. Our Siamese model follows the embedding idea of [8, 9] with the batch-hard triplet loss of [16, 17]. Ageing and drift. A recent subject-disjoint study over eight weekly sessions [12] finds that verification error grows with the gap between enrolment and query for every matcher, including scaled Manhattan, and that matcher choice changes accuracy more than it changes the ageing rate; cross-device drift is addressed by transfer learning in [13]. A survey of concepts and applications is given in [7]. Evaluation methodology. Because entries from the same person are correlated, we estimate uncertainty by resampling subjects (subsets bootstrap [14]), and we use the "biometric zoo" vocabulary of [19] (wolves = impostors who are often accepted) in the error analysis. Reference result. Killourhy and Maxion [1], mean EER over subjects: scaled Manhattan 0.096, Mahalanobis 0.110, Manhattan 0.153, one-class SVM 0.102 (training: first 200 entries; genuine test: remaining 200; impostor test: first 5 entries of each of the other 50 subjects).

3. Datasets

CMU Keystroke Dynamics Benchmark [1] (DSL-StrongPasswordData.csv, cs.cmu.edu/~keystroke). 51 subjects typed the password .tie5Roanl followed by Return, 50 times per session in 8 sessions separated by at least one day: 20,400 entries. Each entry has 31 timing features in seconds: 11 hold times H (key down→up), 10 down-down latencies DD (key down→next key down) and 10 up-down latencies UD (key up→next key down). Subject IDs run s002-s057, 5 IDs absent. A typo made the recording software ask for the password again, so every stored entry is a correctly typed password. Licence: the page states that the data are freely available as a shared resource for public use, asks to be informed of publications and asks that methodologies differing from [1] be labelled as such. We do this: C3 replicates [1]; C1, C2, the ageing curve and the fold protocol differ from it. The data are not redistributed in our code archive; the README explains the download.

Statistics. Mean hold time 90 ms, mean DD latency 249 ms. The median entry takes 2.30 s (1st–99th percentile 1.30–6.69 s, maximum 36.0 s); the per-subject median ranges from 1.41 to 4.93 s. Typing speeds up steadily: the median entry time falls from 2.80 s in session 1 to 2.08 s in session 8, and 49 of 51 subjects are faster in session 8 than in session 1. This practice effect is the main source of cross-session drift.

Quality checks and preprocessing (Phase 3). All structural checks pass (no missing values or duplicates, complete 51×8×50 grid, the identity DD = H + UD holds to 1e-9 s). 10.8% of the UD values are negative (the next key is pressed before the previous one is released); this is genuine rollover behaviour and is kept. 189 entries contain a pause longer than 2 s (longest single gap 26.0 s). Because DD = H + UD, the 31-dimensional covariance has rank 21, so the Mahalanobis detector needs a ridge term. We tested a rejection rule applied to enrolment entries only (discard an entry whose total time exceeds 2× the user's own enrolment median; test entries are never filtered): it removes 77 of 8200 C2 enrolment entries (0.9%), mostly from session 1, and changes the EER by at most a quarter of a percentage point (Table 5). Main results therefore use all entries, which keeps them comparable with [1].

Subject split. The 51 subjects are split once (seed 0) into a tuning group of 10 subjects and an evaluation group of 41. All hyper-parameters (one-class SVM ν, γ; Siamese size and training length) are chosen on the tuning group, and all reported results except the replication use only the 41 evaluation subjects. Own data. No own biometric data are used in the evaluation. For the demo (Section 4.6) we collected typing data from the two team members only, with the instructor's prior approval and the members' explicit consent (a consent box at registration); these entries are stored locally, can be deleted at any time, and are never mixed with the CMU evaluation.

Figure 1. System stages. Higher anomaly score = less like the claimed user. The same code runs the evaluation and the demo.

4.1 Distance detectors (no trained parameters)

For a user with enrolment matrix X (n entries × 31) and mean vector μ, a test vector x is scored by Manhattan Σj|xj−μj|; scaled Manhattan Σj|xj−μj|/aj, where aj is the mean absolute deviation of feature j in the enrolment data, so each feature is measured in units of the user's own variability; and Mahalanobis (x−μ)ᵀ(Σ+λI)⁻¹(x−μ) with λ = 10⁻³·tr(Σ)/31 because Σ is rank-deficient. All three are written in numpy and follow [1].

4.2 One-class SVM (per-user learned model)

Features are z-scored with the enrolment mean and SD of the user, and an RBF one-class SVM [5] (scikit-learn [15] solver) is fitted on the genuine enrolment entries only; the score is the negative decision function. ν and γ were chosen by grid search (ν ∈ {0.01…0.5}, γ ∈ {0.003…0.3}) on the tuning subjects only (sessions 1–3 for training, session 4 for validation): ν = 0.05, γ = 0.03 (tuning EER 10.5%).

4.3 Siamese embedding (learned model shared across users)

H and DD features are log-transformed (they are positive and right-skewed), all features are standardised with statistics of the training subjects, and a multilayer perceptron 31→128→128→128 with ReLU and L2-normalised output maps an entry to an embedding. It is trained in PyTorch [18] with the batch-hard triplet loss [16, 17] (batches of 16 subjects × 16 entries, margin 0.3, Adam, learning rate 10⁻³ with cosine decay, 600 steps): for every anchor, the farthest same-subject entry must be closer than the nearest other-subject entry. Enrolment is cheap: the user's template is the mean embedding of the enrolment entries, and the score is the Euclidean distance to it. Disjointness. The network uses other people as negatives, so (a) the people it is trained on must not be evaluated, and (b) they must not reappear as test impostors. We use 5-fold cross-fitting over the 41 evaluation subjects: for fold f the network is trained on the 10 tuning subjects plus the 4 other folds (all 8 sessions, 43 subjects), and only the 8–9 subjects of fold f are evaluated, with impostors drawn from fold f only. Tuning (18 configurations of size and training length) was done with the network trained on the 41 evaluation subjects and evaluated with protocol C2 on the 10 tuning subjects, so no evaluated person influenced the choice. Longer training over-fitted the small training population (Appendix A).

4.4 Score normalisation and fusion

Raw scores of different detectors are not comparable, so each user's scores are z-normalised with the mean and SD of genuine held-out enrolment scores: in C2 the detector is refitted four times, each time leaving one enrolment session out and scoring it. No impostor and no test data are used. Detector fusion averages the z-scores of scaled Manhattan, one-class SVM and the Siamese embedding. Multi-entry fusion (the optional part of the topic) averages the scores of k consecutive entries of the same session (non-overlapping windows) before the decision, k ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10}.

4.5 Thresholds

The EER is threshold-free (it is computed per user on that condition's test scores and then averaged, as in [1]) and is not an operating point. For an operating point, the threshold is set from enrolment data only: the q-quantile (q = 0.90, 0.95, 0.99) of the user's leave-one-session-out genuine scores; it is then applied unchanged to the test sessions (Table 4).

4.6 Demo system

A Flask web application (proje/demo) records key-down and key-up times in the browser (event.timeStamp), turns an entry into the same H/DD/UD vector (for .tie5Roanl exactly the 31 CMU columns; a unit test replays CMU rows as key events and recovers them exactly), and stores it in SQLite. Like the CMU software, an entry containing Backspace or any editing key is discarded. Only a salted scrypt hash of the password is stored, never the password text; the biometric template is the list of timing vectors (no key text), kept on the local machine and deletable by the user (cascade delete). Login first checks the password hash and then the rhythm with scaled Manhattan + one-class SVM (+ the Siamese network trained on all 51 CMU subjects when the CMU password is used), z-normalised and thresholded exactly as in Sections 4.4–4.5 (leave-one-session-out when the user has two enrolment sessions, otherwise 5-fold cross-validation). An "impostor test" mode lets a team-mate type another member's password; such attempts are logged but never sign anyone in. Screens are shown in Appendix B.

Metrics. DET curve (main curve) and mean per-user EER per condition; per-user EER distributions; FNMR at fixed FMR; 95% bootstrap confidence intervals with 2,000 resamples of subjects, and paired subject resampling for differences between conditions or detectors. Resolution. With 8,000 impostor scores per user, an FMR of 0.1% corresponds to 8 accepted impostor entries, so 0.1% is the lowest FMR we report and DET axes start there; in the fold protocol (≈1443 impostor scores per user) we stop at 1%.

Across sessions, scaled Manhattan (15.1%), Mahalanobis (15.3%) and the one-class SVM (14.3%) are statistically tied (overlapping CIs), and all are far better than plain Manhattan (22.3%), which is dominated by the few long latencies. Scaled Manhattan loses 2.7 pp from C1 to C2 (CI excludes 0) although it is trained on 8× more data in C2, which is direct evidence of drift. Mahalanobis, in contrast, improves from C1 to C2 (-2.9 pp): with only 25 entries its 31×31 covariance is poorly estimated, so in C1 it is limited by training size rather than drift. At practical operating points every detector is weak: at FMR 1%, about half or more of the genuine entries are rejected (Table 2, last columns).

Table 3. All detectors on identical data: 5 folds, impostors only from the evaluated fold (never seen by the Siamese network). k = number of consecutive entries whose scores are averaged.

The fold protocol changes the baselines by less than 0.2 pp, so Tables 2 and 3 are consistent. The Siamese embedding is the best single detector within a session (10.6% vs. 12.2% for scaled Manhattan) but drops to 15.7% across sessions: the largest loss of all detectors (+5.1 pp, CI [3.2, 7.6]). Paired against scaled Manhattan in C2 the difference is +0.7 pp, 95% CI [-1.2, 2.9], i.e. not significant. The embedding learns what separates people at one moment, but the training subjects' own drift is only weakly represented, and the template is a single mean in the embedding space. Fusing the three detectors lowers the C2 EER to 12.7% (-2.3 pp, 95% CI [-6.0, 1.6] vs. scaled Manhattan); the per-user EERs of the detectors are highly rank-correlated (Spearman 0.97 for scaled Manhattan vs. SVM, 0.89 vs. Siamese), which limits what detector fusion can gain. Multi-entry fusion helps much more: averaging 5 entries lowers every detector's EER by 17–38% (relative) (fusion of detectors: 7.1% at k = 5, 6.1% at k = 10), at the cost of asking the user for more entries; in practice this suits a step-up check (ask for one more entry only when the first is borderline).

5.4 Template ageing, operating points and per-user errors

With the enrolment size fixed, the EER rises almost monotonically with the gap: scaled Manhattan from 12.9% (same session) to 24.1% (session 8), the Siamese embedding from 14.3% to 29.4%. This isolates the effect of time from that of training size and agrees with the ageing study [12]. Enrolling over several sessions (C2) partly absorbs the drift, which is why C2 with 200 entries is better than session 8 of this curve.

Thresholds learned on enrolment sessions transfer poorly: a 95% quantile should reject about 5% of genuine entries but accepts 55.6% of impostor entries with scaled Manhattan; the one-class SVM and the Siamese model trade a higher FNMR for a lower FMR at the same q. This is the practical face of drift: a system must either re-enrol or adapt its template, or accept many false matches.

5.5 Error analysis

Users. Errors are concentrated: in C2 with scaled Manhattan, 8 of 41 users have an EER below 5% and 6 above 25%; the 5 worst users (s020, s034, s032, s007, s051, EER 29–40%) account for 28% of the summed error. Because the rank correlation across detectors is high, these are hard users for every detector (Doddington's "goats" [19]), not failures of one method. Impostors. Some impostors are "wolves": at each target's EER threshold, the median impostor subject is accepted 11% of the time, but s026 and s029 are accepted 52% and 45% of the time on average, i.e. their typing resembles many others'. Features. Measured in each user's own enrolment SDs, hold times drift most (mean |shift| 0.48 SD vs. 0.34 for DD and 0.36 for UD); the largest shifts are at the e→5 transition (letter to digit row). Every evaluated user types faster in sessions 5–8 than in 1–4 (median ratio 0.83). The per-user amount of drift correlates only weakly with the per-user C2 EER (Spearman ρ = 0.24, p = 0.13, not significant): users who are hard to verify are often inconsistent within a session or simply similar to others, not only drifting.

Table 6. Replication of the reference protocol (C3). The one-class SVM is reported on the 41 evaluation subjects only, because its hyper-parameters were tuned on the other 10.

The three distance detectors reproduce [1] to within 0.1 pp (9.6 / 11.1 / 15.3% vs. 9.6 / 11.0 / 15.3%), which validates our feature handling, detectors and EER computation. Our one-class SVM is 1.4 pp worse than in [1]: the reference used its own SVM implementation and parameter choice, whereas our ν, γ were selected for cross-session validation on 10 subjects; its confidence interval [9.5, 14.1] still contains the reference value. Two differences in protocol explain why our C2 numbers are about 5 pp higher than the reference: C3 tests each impostor only on their first 5 entries, typed before any practice with the password, which makes impostors easy to reject, whereas C1/C2 test impostors on practised entries from the same sessions as the genuine test; and C2 tests later sessions than it trains on. The ranking of the distance detectors (scaled Manhattan < Mahalanobis < Manhattan) is the same in [1] and in all of our conditions, and we confirm the reference finding that scaling by per-feature variability matters most. Accuracy reported with cross-validation on this dataset [11] is not comparable to either.

7. Limitations

  • Statistical power. 41 evaluation subjects give wide confidence intervals (about ±3 pp on C2 EERs); differences of 1–2 pp between the better detectors cannot be resolved. The fold protocol has fewer impostor comparisons, so FMR below 1% is not reported for it.
  • One password, one population, one keyboard. All subjects typed the same 10-character password in a lab; results may not transfer to other passwords, keyboards or mobile devices [13], or to impostors who have watched and practised the victim's rhythm.
  • Drift is confounded with practice. The CMU sessions start with an unfamiliar password; part of the drift is learning, which would be smaller for a long-used password and larger over months [12].
  • Siamese model. A small MLP on ≈41 training subjects; a larger population, session-aware training (positives from different sessions) or template updating would likely help in C2. The model was selected among 18 configurations; we did not test other architectures.
  • Thresholds. Enrolment-based thresholds do not account for future drift; the EER is a summary, not a deployable operating point.
  • Demo. Browser timestamps are coarser and noisier than the CMU clock, there are only a few self-declared trials, and the template is stored unprotected (no template protection or encryption at rest). The demo shows the pipeline; it is not evidence of accuracy.

8. Conclusions

On the CMU benchmark we reproduced the reference results of [1] and showed that within-session evaluation is optimistic. Across sessions, scaled Manhattan, Mahalanobis and a one-class SVM reach about 14–15% mean EER, statistically tied; plain Manhattan is clearly worse. A Siamese embedding shared across users and trained on disjoint subjects is the best detector within a session but the most sensitive to drift, so a learned model's within-session advantage did not carry over to later sessions. With a fixed enrolment size the EER grows steadily with the time gap, and enrolment-based thresholds admit many impostors in later sessions. The two most effective improvements are ones that add information rather than model capacity: enrolling over several sessions, and fusing several consecutive entries (≈ 7% EER for five entries with three detectors). Keystroke rhythm is therefore a useful, cheap second factor on top of a password, best used with step-up verification and template updating, but not a stand-alone authenticator.

AI Use Declaration

Tools: Claude Code (Anthropic; Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the design-document phase, Claude Opus 5.5 for the final phase) and web search through it. Used for: writing and debugging Python code (detectors, evaluation protocols, metrics, bootstrap, Siamese network and cross-fitting, figures), the Flask/SQLite demo and its JavaScript key capture, generating this report's and the slides' layout from the result files, searching and summarising literature, and language editing. How we checked the output: the implementation was validated by reproducing the published results of [1] (Section 6); the demo's feature extraction is tested by replaying CMU rows as key events and recovering the exact feature vectors, and the demo flows were tested end to end with real keyboard events in a browser; every number in this report is generated from the JSON files written by reproduce.py, which we re-ran; the split rules (tuning vs. evaluation subjects, fold-disjoint training and impostors, enrolment-only thresholds) were checked against the project description and topic A5; every reference was looked up online (authors, title, venue, year) and re-opened by us before submission. We can explain every part of the code and results.
